The Chains Aren’t Eating Montréal. They’re Moving.

Fourteen years of city food-inspection records show chains losing ground downtown, spreading into the suburbs, and doing no measurable harm to the independents next door.

By Zachary D. Lewin · November 2026 · Analysis of 54,893 food-business records from the City of Montréal, 2012 to 2026

When I first arrived in Montréal, there was a 24-hour café-bar I fell in love with. On the corner of Milton and Parc, it looked like a Canadian barn, and at any hour you could go in for a decently priced coffee and pastry, or a beer or a cocktail in the evening. At all hours there were people studying, couples on dates, friends hanging out, and homeless people coming in for shelter from the storms. It was a genuinely kind and inviting place. This year it changed hands. I assumed a chain had swallowed it. It hadn’t: the small café across the street had taken it over, and it no longer stays open all night.

It’s the story every city tells about itself: the chains move in and the corner shops die. Montréal now keeps good records to test it. The city inspects every place that sells food, from cafés and bakeries to dépanneurs and fast-food counters, and logs when each one opens, changes hands or closes for good.

Those records tell a different story.

In 2012, chains made up 9.5 percent of the city’s food businesses. They peaked at 10.9 percent in 2018 and have slipped back since. This year they are at 9.5 percent again, about 990 out of 10,400. By that measure, the takeover never happened.

But the city-wide total hides a shift in where the chains really are.

Watch downtown and the pattern is hard to miss. Through the 2010s the core held about 300 chain locations, many of them sandwich counters and coffee chains. After 2020, a quarter of them went dark and didn’t come back: from 291 to 217. Meanwhile new orange dots kept appearing further out, along the commercial strips of Ahuntsic, Rivière-des-Prairies and the Sud-Ouest.

Downtown Ville-Marie fell the most, from 13.8 to 10.4 percent, a drop of 3.4 points. The chains grew in the Sud-Ouest, from 4.4 to 6.6 percent, and in the outer boroughs: Rivière-des-Prairies, Ahuntsic-Cartierville, Côte-des-Neiges.

The Plateau has more food businesses than any borough outside downtown, and only about one in 20 is a chain: 4.9 percent, barely changed since 2013. It remains the most independent part of the city, and in 2025 Time Out ranked the Plateau and its Mile End enclave among the 25 coolest neighbourhoods in the world.

The chain that grew most is Couche-Tard, the convenience store founded in Laval in 1980: from 103 locations to 141, filling in gaps wherever it could across the whole island.

The new chains are increasingly local. Boustan opened on Crescent Street in 1986 and stayed essentially a single downtown counter for more than two decades. After a 2012 sale it began franchising, and it now has 16 locations on the island, almost all of them outside downtown.

Downtown’s losses came from the brands that once defined it. Subway went from 124 locations to 92 across the city, and Second Cup from 32 to 15. The gainers are newer and often smaller: sushi counters, poke bowls, bubble tea, and Montréal’s own Boustan.

What happens next door

The harder question is what a chain does to its neighbours. To test it, I took each of the 673 chain locations that opened between 2012 and mid-2024 and looked at the independent food businesses around it, comparing those within 150 metres, about a block, with those 300 to 800 metres away, in the same part of town but out of the chain’s immediate reach.

Then I measured how many of each closed for good in the two years after the chain arrived, and in the two years before. Here is what that looks like for a single opening.

Independents a block from a new chain were already closing a little more often than those further away before it arrived: 12.6 percent versus 11.7 percent over two years. After it arrived, the gap disappeared: 12.1 versus 12.4. Relative to their own past, the nearby shops did about one percentage point better.

It’s a small effect, and it isn’t proof that chains help. The likelier explanation is that chains choose their corners carefully, opening where foot traffic is already rising, and that rising tide lifts the shops around them too. What the data does not show is the opposite: no sign that a new chain pushes its neighbours out of business.

I ran the same test on narrower matchups: independent cafés next to new coffee chains, independent grocers next to new Couche-Tards, and ownership changes rather than closures. None showed a clear effect once corrected for running several tests at once. Only the overall result held up.

A city that keeps its corners

Montréal is a special city, with its own culture and its own tastes. The chains that open here and stay are, more and more, homegrown, a sign of how much Montrealers love what is local. And the independents that open here do so with a dream of growing. Montréal is not a city that pushes out the old to force in the new. It adapts, organically.

About the data

Records come from the City of Montréal’s open dataset of food establishments under its inspection, downloaded in November 2026: 54,893 records, each with a name, address, type, status (open, closed, changed owner) and the date of its latest status. The analysis keeps consumer-facing types (restaurants, fast food, cafés, bakeries, grocers, butchers, bars and similar) on the island of Montréal. Brand names were standardised, and a chain is any brand with at least 10 locations in the records; gas-station counters, pharmacies and generic names such as “Dépanneur du Coin” were excluded.

The dataset gives the date of each business’s latest status, not its opening date. The city assigns identification numbers in sequence, and since 2011 those numbers rise steadily with time, so opening dates were estimated from each record’s ID. Checked against businesses listed as recently opened, the estimate has a median error of 28 days. Records entered before 2011 are treated as already open.

The neighbour comparison is a difference-in-differences: change in two-year closure rates for independents within 150 m of a new chain, minus the same change for independents 300–800 m away, with 95 percent intervals from 400 bootstrap resamples of chain openings. P-values for the four tests were adjusted with the Holm method (Holm, 1979). Overall effect: −1.1 percentage points (95% interval −2.0 to −0.2), the only result significant after adjustment. Closure dates record when the city learned of a closure, which may lag the actual date.

Other sources: Boustan’s history (Wikipedia, Montreal Mirror); Time Out’s 2025 ranking of the world’s coolest neighbourhoods. Borough boundaries: Ville de Montréal open data. Analysis in Python and DuckDB; graphics in D3.
